💡 Strengthening Startup Innovation Through Intellectual Property Awareness!

IIT Mandi Catalyst recently hosted an insightful workshop on Intellectual Property (IP) for Startups, aimed at enhancing awareness of IP protection, strategic management and its role in building and scaling innovative ventures.

The session was led by Mr. Rajashekhar S, Management & Technology Consultant, who shared valuable insights into key aspects of IP strategy and protection.

🔍 Key Highlights of the Workshop:
🔹 Understanding IP frameworks and different types of IP protection.
🔹 Exploring corporate IP divisions and the end-to-end IP filing workflow.
🔹 Developing effective IP strategies and risk management approaches for startups.
🔹 Analysing patent landscapes to identify opportunities and assess the competitive ecosystem.
🔹 Understanding provisional patent filing strategies, particularly for hardware startups.

The workshop provided valuable perspectives on protecting innovations, navigating the IP landscape and leveraging intellectual property as a strategic asset for startups.

At IIT Mandi Catalyst, we remain committed to empowering startups with the knowledge and resources needed to strengthen their innovations and build sustainable businesses.

This international recognition marks a significant milestone for LOGOJECH Technologies, reflecting its growing global ambitions and the potential of Indian deep-tech innovation to address real-world industrial challenges.

At IIT Mandi Catalyst, we take pride in seeing our incubated startups expand their horizons, build international networks and explore opportunities beyond national boundaries.

Meet EternaSafe, founded by Amardeep Kumar, an IIT Mandi Catalyst-incubated startup working to redefine how individuals prepare for their family's financial and personal continuity.

EternaSafe is a secure digital platform that helps individuals organise, store, track and manage their important personal, financial and business information.

Built around the concept of "𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞," EternaSafe addresses an important question: What happens to all the information you know, if one day you are unable to guide your family?

EternaSafe is designed around two important purposes:

𝟏. 𝐘𝐎𝐔𝐑 𝐈𝐍𝐅𝐎𝐑𝐌𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍. 𝐘𝐎𝐔𝐑 𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐓𝐑𝐎𝐋.
Organise and manage your critical life-related information in one private, encrypted platform. You don't have to share your information with anyone. EternaSafe's zero-knowledge architecture is designed so that even the platform cannot read your encrypted vault data.

𝟐. 𝐘𝐎𝐔𝐑 𝐅𝐀𝐌𝐈𝐋𝐘. 𝐘𝐎𝐔𝐑 𝐏𝐑𝐄𝐏𝐀𝐑𝐀𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍.
If an unexpected situation leaves you unable to respond, EternaSafe's inactivity monitoring and verification process is designed to facilitate controlled access to your prepared information for your pre-designated nominee, following the required identity verification and checks.

✨𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐄𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐒𝐚𝐟𝐞?
🔒𝐏𝐑𝐈𝐕𝐀𝐓𝐄 𝐁𝐘 𝐃𝐄𝐒𝐈𝐆𝐍: Your encrypted information remains inaccessible to EternaSafe.
📂𝐎𝐑𝐆𝐀𝐍𝐈𝐒𝐄𝐃 𝐅𝐎𝐑 𝐋𝐈𝐅𝐄: Keep track of important personal, financial and business information in one place.
🛡️𝐏𝐑𝐄𝐏𝐀𝐑𝐄𝐃 𝐅𝐎𝐑 𝐔𝐍𝐂𝐄𝐑𝐓𝐀𝐈𝐍𝐓𝐘: Set up a process for your family to access the information you have prepared when needed.
❤️𝐏𝐄𝐀𝐂𝐄 𝐎𝐅 𝐌𝐈𝐍𝐃: Your family may not always have you beside them, but they can have the guidance you prepared.

EternaSafe: Your information, your control. Your family's guidance, when it matters most.

#SkinInTheGame | Post 3 of 3
Last week, I shared my criticism of some aspects of the development sector in two posts —
1. The lanyard/conference culture — https://lnkd.in/gxhBymrJ
2. The systems change fallacy without skin in the game — https://lnkd.in/gtnZAMiW

Now sharing the third and hopefully last post in this series —

The Development Sector Needs a Higher Standard. Not a Lower One.

A question I am sometimes asked is why I hold the development sector to a standard I do not apply to the business world. The answer rests on a single, uncomfortable fact: in business, the people whose money is being spent have agency. In the development sector, they do not.

Markets, over time, punish poor capital discipline. In the development sector, the logic is inverted. The TB patient cannot fire the globe-trotting consultant. The smallholder farmer cannot question the panel debating her livelihood. The forest cannot seek a refund from a carbon credit peddler. This is not a minor distinction. It is a moral asymmetry of the first order.

And yet the waste has not merely persisted. It has been institutionalised.
The elite nonprofit complex is now a recognisable feature of the landscape: well-resourced organisations in premium offices, generously compensated executives, a packed calendar of convenings and summits, and alongside them, a consulting industry that does not merely serve the sector but actively shapes its language, its frameworks, and its definition of credibility. These firms are paid by the same organisations whose strategies they assess. The incentive, therefore, is never to disrupt. It is to validate, to elaborate, and to return next year. The result is a closed loop of institutional comfort dressed in the vocabulary of transformation.

I am not arguing that the business world is above critique. It externalises vast social and environmental costs that never appear on a balance sheet. But within its own internal logic, it at least has mechanisms that correct for waste. The development sector has none. Which is precisely why those of us who work within it carry a higher obligation — to insist on rigour, to challenge performative activity, and to refuse the comfortable consensus that good intentions are a substitute for results. The cost of our self-indulgence is paid in the lives of people and the planet.

The development sector exists because the market failed the people it serves. That is not a reason to hold it to a lower standard than the world it critiques. It is the most compelling reason imaginable to hold it to a higher one.

#SkinInTheGame #Accountability #Development #Philanthropy #SocialImpact

Bringing together ideas, expertise, and on-ground experience, Social Alpha brought together founders, policymakers, and ecosystem partners in Bhubaneswar at a convening titled Innovation to Impact: Strategy, Growth & Scale, exploring pathways for scaling innovation across agriculture, animal husbandry, and rural livelihoods.

Shri Shubhranshu Mishra, Additional Secretary, Department of Agriculture & Farmers’ Empowerment, Government of Odisha, shared his insights about Odisha’s potential as a hub for agricultural innovation and the need to strengthen the ecosystem for innovators and farmers.
A fireside chat between Dr Soumya Swaminathan, Chairperson, MSSRF, and Social Alpha founder, Manoj Kumar explored what it takes to move innovations from research to scale. The focus was on creating measurable value for farmers through higher incomes, reduced drudgery, and greater inclusion of women in agriculture.
Dr Rajesh Gupta, Senior General Manager (Productivity Enhancement), NDDB, spoke on strengthening dairy systems through improved breeding practices, balanced cattle nutrition, and feed management.
 
Innovation founders brought solutions across data-driven farming, blended finance, animal health, and livestock productivity to the table. Discussions also unpacked the challenges that often stand between a promising innovation and its adoption at scale, including farmer trust, access to finance, after-sales support, supply chains, and last-mile implementation.
Central to building an innovation ecosystem are solutions not only developed but also tested, adopted, and scaled to create lasting value for farmers and rural communities.
 
#InnovationForImpact #Agritech #SmallholderFarmers #AnimalHusbandry #RuralLivelihoods #InnovationEcosystem #SocialAlpha

Neeraj Jain | Ganesh Neelam | Dr Kavita Singh | Harish Hande

What does it take for an innovation to actually reach the people it was designed to serve?

Sometimes, the biggest barrier isn't the technology. It's everything that needs to happen around it.

During a field visit, a woman farmer in Hatipur handed over ₹10 to the team behind an initiative that had brought new technologies to her community. It wasn't a payment or charity, but a blessing, a reciprocal gesture of gratitude for the economic independence those innovations had helped create.

For Onkar Pandey, Director at Social Alpha, this is what meaningful impact looks like: solutions that respond to real needs and create value for the communities they are designed to serve.

In the second episode of Voices of Value, we draw on Onkar's more than two decades of experience in the development sector to explore what it takes to move agricultural innovations beyond research institutions and pilot projects and into the hands of farmers.

Our conversation looks at why promising technologies often struggle to scale, the role of financing, distribution and after-sales support, and how collaboration between farmers, governments and philanthropic institutions can help build the ecosystems needed for adoption.

Onkar also shares a simple but important piece of advice for early-stage social entrepreneurs:

“Solve the problem. Revenue will chase you.”

A perspective that puts the focus where it belongs: on understanding the problem, earning the trust of communities and building solutions that can sustain themselves over time.

UN Global Compact Network India is delighted to welcome Entrepreneurship Development Center as its participant!

They are a national award-winning, not-for-profit deep-tech and science-based business incubator, hosted by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research – National Chemical Laboratory (CSIR-NCL), Pune. Established in 2007, it nurtures knowledge-based enterprises emerging from science and technology, helping innovators translate research and discoveries into market-ready products, technologies and ventures.

Working at the intersection of science, entrepreneurship and societal impact, the Center provides a comprehensive support ecosystem comprising incubation, mentorship, early-stage funding, specialized scientific and analytical facilities, prototyping infrastructure, technical and business advisory, and networking opportunities.

Its focus areas include healthcare and rehabilitation, energy and environment, and engineering and automation, with an emphasis on enabling innovations in climate action, clean energy, circular economy and food security. Through science-led entrepreneurship, the Center aims to foster solutions that create meaningful economic, environmental and societal impact.

Learn more about Entrepreneurship Development Center’s commitment to responsible business through its UN Global Compact participant profile.

We’re delighted to share that BabyCue Pvt Ltd, an iCreate portfolio startup, has won 1st Prize at the Tribal Business Conclave Open Grand Challenge, along with a ₹5 lakh cash award! 

Organised by the MINISTRY OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS GOVERNMENT OF INDIA (MoTA), in association with Startup India, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, the challenge recognised BabyCue for its innovative contribution to healthcare.

Through its product DiaCue, BabyCue is advancing rapid diagnostics by helping distinguish bacterial from non-bacterial diarrhoea, supporting timely and informed treatment decisions.

Congratulations to Team BabyCue on this achievement!
